claim: Short-term memory is considered to be a critical component of general intelligence.
source: Short-term memory, which refers to the brain's temporary buffer of readily usable information, is considered to be a critical component of general intelligence (Conway et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Conway et al., 2003

claim: Human working memory involves short-term memory, executive selection and processing, operating on multiple timescales and across multiple brain areas.
source: Human working memory is a complex phenomenon, involving not just short-term memory but executive selection and processing, operating on multiple timescales and across multiple brain areas (Jonides et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jonides et al., 2008

claim: Memory capacity is restricted to just a handful of items.
source: Consistent with everyday experience, memory capacity is severely limited, restricted to just a handful of items (Miller, 1956), and recall performance is worse when there are more items to be remembered.
evidence: Supported by citation to Miller, 1956

claim: Recall performance is worse when there are more items to be remembered.
source: Consistent with everyday experience, memory capacity is severely limited, restricted to just a handful of items (Miller, 1956), and recall performance is worse when there are more items to be remembered.
evidence: Supported by citation to Miller, 1956 and general knowledge

claim: Several experiments show that recall performance declines with delay when many items are stored in memory.
source: several experiments show that recall performance declines with delay (Luck and Vogel, 1997; Jonides et al., 2008; Barrouillet et al., 2009; Barrouillet et al., 2011; Barrouillet et al., 2012; Pertzov et al., 2013; Wilken and Ma, 2004; Bays et al., 2011; Pertzov et al., 2017; Anderson et al., 2011), at least when many items are stored in memory.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to experimental studies

claim: Persistent neural activity has been widely hypothesized to form the substrate for short-term memory.
source: On the mechanistic side, persistent neural activity has been widely hypothesized to form the substrate for short-term memory.
evidence: Supported by general knowledge in the field

claim: There is a link between short-term memory and persistent neural activity established by electrophysiological work.
source: The hypothesis is based on a corpus of electrophysiological work establishing a link between short-term memory and persistent neural activity (Funahashi, 2006; Smith and Jonides, 1998; Wimmer et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to electrophysiological studies

claim: Neural network models of analog persistent activity predict a degradation of information over time because of noise in synaptic and neural activation.
source: Neural network models of analog persistent activity predict a degradation of information over time (Compte et al., 2000; Brody et al., 2003; Boucheny et al., 2005; Burak and Fiete, 2009; Fung et al., 2010; Mongillo et al., 2008; Burak and Fiete, 2012; Wei et al., 2012), because of noise in synaptic and neural activation.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to neural network modeling studies

claim: Response accuracy degraded significantly with delay duration when there were 6 items in the stimulus.
source: By contrast, response accuracy degraded significantly with delay duration when there were 6 items in the stimulus (Figure 1C; true orientation subtracted from all responses to provide a common center at 0 degrees).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: In ring attractor networks, all rotations of the canonical activity bump form a one-dimensional continuum of steady states.
source: All rotations of the canonical activity bump form a one-dimensional continuum of steady states, Figure 2B.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of ring attractor networks and illustrated in Figure 2B

claim: Noise in network activity leads to lateral random drift along the manifold in the form of a diffusive (Ornstein-Uhlenbeck) random walk.
source: However, any noise in network activity, for instance in form of stochastic spiking (Softky and Koch, 1993; Shadlen and Newsome, 1994), leads to lateral random drift along the manifold in the form of a diffusive (Ornstein-Uhlenbeck) random walk (Compte et al., 2000; Brody et al., 2003; Boucheny et al., 2005; Wu et al., 2008; Burak and Fiete, 2009; Fung et al., 2010; Burak and Fiete, 2012), Figure 2C–D.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations and illustrated in Figure 2C-D

claim: The diffusivity of the state in persistent activity networks scales as the inverse of the number of neurons and of the peak firing rate per neuron.
source: We know from (Burak and Fiete, 2012) that the diffusivity of the state in each of these 1D persistent activity networks will scale as the inverse of the number of neurons and of the peak firing rate per neuron.
evidence: Supported by citation to Burak and Fiete, 2012

claim: Well-coded storage requires substantially fewer resources in the persistent activity networks for similar performance compared to direct storage.
source: Thus, well-coded storage requires substantially fewer resources in the persistent activity networks for similar performance (assuming best fits of each produce similar performance).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of resource requirements between models

claim: A memory system with good encoding can achieve substantially better performance with the same total storage resources than if information were directly stored in persistent activity networks.
source: Equivalently, a memory system with good encoding can achieve substantially better performance with the same total storage resources, than if information were directly stored in persistent activity networks.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of model performance

claim: Neural responses for short-term memory are diverse and do not exhibit tuning that is as simple or uniform as typical for classical population codes.
source: Intriguingly, neural responses for short-term memory are diverse and do not exhibit tuning that is as simple or uniform as typical for classical population codes (Miller et al., 1996; Fuster and Alexander, 1971; Romo et al., 1999; Wang, 2001; Funahashi, 2006; Fuster and Jervey, 1981; Rigotti et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to neurophysiological studies

claim: All subjects reported normal or corrected-to-normal visual acuity.
source: All subjects reported normal or corrected-to-normal visual acuity.
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: According to the well-coded storage bound, increasing the number of stored items degrades performance much more steeply than increasing the storage interval because item number is in the exponent.
source: Second, the scaling with item number is qualitatively different than the scaling with storage duration: Increasing the number of stored items degrades performance much more steeply than increasing the storage interval, because item number is in the exponent.
evidence: Inferred from the mathematical form of Equation 2

claim: For a single memorized feature or item, the decline in accuracy with storage interval duration is predicted to be weak in the well-coded model.
source: For a single memorized feature or item, the decline in accuracy with storage interval duration is predicted to be weak.
evidence: Inferred from the mathematical form of Equation 2

claim: The degradation of information stored directly in persistent activity networks behaves differently from human short-term memory performance.
source: Yet, as we show, the degradation of information stored directly in such networks behaves differently from human short-term memory performance.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparison of model predictions to experimental data

claim: If the brain first encoded the information appropriately before passing the information into persistent activity networks, the information can be stored substantially more faithfully.
source: If the brain first encoded the information appropriately before passing the information into such networks, the information can be stored substantially more faithfully.
evidence: Inferred from information-theoretic analysis

claim: Human performance is inconsistent with models involving direct (uncoded) storage in persistent activity networks.
source: We show that human performance, though inconsistent with models involving direct (uncoded) storage in persistent activity networks, can be well-fit by the theoretical bound.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparison of model predictions to experimental data

claim: Human performance can be well-fit by the theoretical bound from well-coded storage.
source: We show that human performance, though inconsistent with models involving direct (uncoded) storage in persistent activity networks, can be well-fit by the theoretical bound.
evidence: Demonstrated by fitting theoretical bound to experimental data

claim: If the brain stores information in patterns of persistent activity, it might use codes that minimize the effects of noise.
source: This finding is consistent with the view that if the brain stores information in patterns of persistent activity, it might use codes that minimize the effects of noise, motivating the search for such codes in the brain.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the fit of the well-coded model to data
